primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Pituitary apoplexy with acute secondary adrenal insufficiency
mechanism: Sudden hemorrhage or infarction within the pituitary gland, often in a pre-existing adenoma, can abruptly impair ACTH secretion. The resulting cortisol deficiency reduces vascular responsiveness to vasoconstrictors and promotes nonosmotic ADH activity, causing hypotension and hyponatremia; aldosterone secretion is relatively preserved because it is regulated primarily by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and serum potassium.
vignette: A 47-year-old man with a known nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma develops an abrupt severe retro-orbital headache, vomiting, diplopia, and left-sided ptosis. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L, potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, and glucose is 61 mg/dL. MRI shows acute hemorrhagic infarction within the pituitary mass with suprasellar expansion.
lead: Which endocrine mechanism most directly explains this patient’s hemodynamic instability and electrolyte pattern?
correct: Abrupt ACTH deficiency causing cortisol deficiency, with relatively preserved aldosterone secretion
distractors: Destruction of the adrenal cortex causing simultaneous cortisol and aldosterone deficiency
Loss of posterior pituitary ADH secretion causing renal free-water loss and hypovolemia
Abrupt TSH deficiency causing severe hypothyroidism as the primary cause of shock
Excess ACTH secretion causing cortisol-mediated suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
distractor_notes: Primary adrenal cortical destruction can cause cortisol and aldosterone deficiency with hyperkalemia and volume depletion. This patient has a pituitary lesion causing secondary adrenal insufficiency, in which aldosterone is generally preserved.
Loss of ADH causes central diabetes insipidus with polyuria and a tendency toward hypernatremia, not this hyponatremic pattern.
TSH deficiency can contribute to chronic central hypothyroidism but does not explain the immediate life-threatening hypotension of acute pituitary apoplexy as directly as ACTH/cortisol loss.
Pituitary apoplexy causes loss rather than excess of ACTH in the relevant emergency. Excess cortisol would not produce the acute cortisol-deficient shock physiology shown.
key_expl: This patient has pituitary apoplexy: sudden hemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary macroadenoma causing abrupt headache, ophthalmoplegia, and endocrine failure. The most dangerous acute endocrine consequence is secondary adrenal insufficiency from loss of ACTH. Cortisol deficiency decreases vascular responsiveness to angiotensin II and catecholamines and can increase ADH-mediated water retention, producing hypotension and hyponatremia. Aldosterone is usually preserved because zona glomerulosa secretion is controlled mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and serum potassium rather than ACTH. Therefore potassium can remain normal, helping distinguish secondary from primary adrenal insufficiency.
objective: In pituitary apoplexy, recognize acute ACTH deficiency as the critical cause of secondary adrenal insufficiency and distinguish it from primary adrenal failure by relative preservation of aldosterone and potassium balance.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Pituitary Apoplexy — StatPearls
sources.locator: Continuing Education Activity; Introduction; History and Physical; Treatment/Management
sources.support: NCBI states that pituitary apoplexy results from sudden hemorrhage or infarction, frequently in a pituitary adenoma, presents with abrupt headache/visual deficits/ophthalmoplegia, and that acute adrenal insufficiency is the most immediate life-threatening complication requiring prompt corticosteroid replacement.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Pituitary Apoplexy — Endotext
sources.locator: Clinical Recognition; Pathophysiology; Radiologic and Laboratory Evaluation; Treatment
sources.support: Endotext describes hemorrhage/infarction with abrupt sellar expansion, cavernous-sinus cranial nerve palsies, hyponatremia and low cortisol, and identifies acute secondary adrenal insufficiency as the major source of mortality in pituitary apoplexy.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Diagnosis and Management of Adrenal Insufficiency — Endotext
sources.support: Endotext states that ACTH deficiency causes low cortisol while mineralocorticoid production remains normal because aldosterone is principally regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis; hypotension can still occur from reduced vascular responsiveness to angiotensin II and norepinephrine.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: ACTH Action on the Adrenals — Endotext
sources.locator: Effects of ACTH on Adrenal Cortical Cells
sources.support: Endotext explains that ACTH is the main stimulus for zona fasciculata cortisol secretion, whereas angiotensin II and potassium are the main regulators of aldosterone secretion by the zona glomerulosa.
